Twitch: guide for parents and educators (official)
Twitch: viewer controls and content labels (official)

twitch.noKidsAlt: Twitch's terms say the service is not available under 13 at all, so there is no younger version to move to.

netflix.name: Netflix
netflix.blurb: A kids profile is easy to make and does very little on its own. What matters is locking the adult profiles, because otherwise your child is two taps away from all of them.
risks: A kids profile is pointless if the adult profiles have no PIN, and profile locks are off by default
Each adult profile has to be locked separately
A Kids profile's rating cannot be raised later, and Netflix's fix is to delete it and lose the history
beforeYouStart: Do this on a computer or in the mobile app. Most of it cannot be done from the TV app.
You'll need your Netflix password a few times.

steps.title: Make them their own profile
steps.why: Ratings, autoplay and history are all set per profile, so a shared profile means none of it applies.
steps.path: Manage Profiles → Add Profile → For Kids
do: Open Manage Profiles, then Add Profile.
Name it, and tick the For Kids box for younger children.
On a TV the label may read Kids Profile rather than For Kids.
steps.note: The main account profile cannot be turned into a kids profile, and there is a limit of five profiles.

steps.title: Set the maturity rating
steps.why: This is the main content control, and it applies to Netflix games as well as films and shows. Two things to watch. Setting a rating above the kids level switches off the kid-safe experience along with it. And a Kids profile that Netflix created automatically when you opened the account cannot be raised at all, so if you need a higher level you have to delete it and make a new profile.
steps.path: Account → Profiles → Adjust parental controls
do: Go to Account, then Profiles, then Adjust parental controls.
Pick the profile and verify it's you.
Set the maturity rating and save.
steps.note: Rating names vary by country. These are the US names; in the UK and Ireland you'll see BBFC ratings in the same place.

steps.title: Lock every adult profile with a PIN
steps.why: This is the step almost everyone misses, and without it the rest is decoration. A child who can tap back to your profile has no restrictions at all.
steps.path: Account → Profiles → [adult profile] → Profile Lock
do: Go to Account, then Profiles, then pick an adult profile.
Choose Profile Lock, then Create a Profile Lock.
Set a 4-digit PIN and save.
Repeat for every adult profile on the account.
steps.result: Your child can no longer switch into an unrestricted profile.
steps.note: On the main profile you can also turn on Require a PIN to add a new profile, which stops them making a fresh unrestricted one. Note that Extra Member accounts cannot use profile locks at all.

steps.title: Block specific titles if you need to
steps.why: Netflix is the only one of the big streamers that lets you block an individual show.
steps.path: Account → Profiles → Adjust parental controls → Title Restrictions
do: On the same parental controls screen, find Title Restrictions.
Type the title and select it.
Save.

steps.title: Turn off autoplay
steps.why: Autoplay is what turns one episode into an evening, and the previews are what put things in front of them they were not looking for. It is set per profile, so switching it off on theirs leaves yours alone.
steps.path: Account → Profiles → [child] → Playback settings
do: Go to Account, then Profiles, then the child's profile, then Playback settings.
Turn off Autoplay previews and Autoplay next episode.

steps.title: Add a device-level backstop
steps.why: These settings only cover this one service. A device-level control catches the app they download next.
do: Set up Screen Time, Family Link, Microsoft Family Safety or your console's own controls.
Require your approval for new app downloads.
steps.note: SafeStart has a separate guide for each of these. Pick your device on the home screen.

checklist: Maturity rating set for their age
Every adult profile has a PIN
talkAboutIt: Watch the first episode of something new with them rather than vetting it alone.
Agree what they do if something they start makes them uncomfortable: stop it and tell you.

links.label: Netflix: maturity ratings and blocking titles (official)

kidsAlt.name: A Kids profile
kidsAlt.what: Tick “For Kids” when you add a profile. It has a simpler layout, blocks access to account settings, and has no email of its own, so nobody can sign in with it directly.
kidsAlt.watchOut: Setting a maturity rating above the kids level quietly switches the kid-safe features off. Put a profile lock PIN on your own profile too, or they will just tap across to it.

disneyplus.name: Disney+
disneyplus.blurb: Junior Mode is a solid walled garden for young children. The setting that catches people out is the one allowing unrated live sports and news, which is on by default and includes its ad breaks.
risks: Unrated live content is allowed by default on every profile that isn't in Junior Mode
The main profile defaults to the highest rating and cannot be put in Junior Mode
Junior Mode is all or nothing, with no middle setting for an older child
beforeYouStart: You can only change these on a web browser or in the mobile app, not on the TV app.
Have your Disney+ password ready. Most of these steps ask for it.

steps.title: Turn on Junior Mode for younger children
steps.why: This is the kids profile, renamed. If you go looking for Kids Profile in the app you won't find it.
steps.path: Edit Profiles → [profile] → Parental Controls → Junior Mode
do: Go to your profiles and choose Add Profile, or Edit Profiles for one that exists.
Pick an avatar and name it.
Under Parental Controls, switch Junior Mode on.
Save.
steps.note: Junior Mode profiles see no ads. The main profile cannot be put into Junior Mode, and turning Junior Mode off needs your password.

steps.title: Set the content rating for an older child
steps.why: For a child too old for the all-ages walled garden, the rating is the only content lever, because Junior Mode has nothing to adjust. This is where families tend to give up: Junior Mode feels babyish to a 10 or 11 year old, so it gets switched off and nothing takes its place. A rating on an ordinary profile is the middle option that actually survives.
steps.path: Edit Profiles → [profile] → Parental Controls → Content rating
do: Go to your profiles, choose Edit Profiles, and select the profile.
Under Parental Controls choose Content rating.
Enter your password, pick the rating, and save.
steps.note: Rating names vary by country. These are the US names; in the UK and Ireland you'll see BBFC ratings in the same place.

steps.title: Turn off unrated live content
steps.why: This is the one that catches people out. It is on by default, and Disney's own warning is blunt: live content and live ads may feature adult themes, products and services. Setting a child's profile to a low rating and stopping there leaves live sports, live news and their ad breaks wide open.
steps.path: Edit Profiles → [profile] → Parental Controls → allow titles without ratings
do: On the same Parental Controls screen for the profile, find the setting allowing titles without ratings, such as live sports and news.
Turn it off.
steps.result: Unrated live content and its ads no longer appear on that profile.
steps.note: Turning it back on later needs your password. Turning it off does not.

steps.title: Put a PIN on your own profile
steps.why: The main profile defaults to the highest rating, so without a PIN your child switches into it in two taps.
steps.path: Edit Profiles → [your profile] → Parental Controls → Profile PIN
do: Go to your profiles, choose Edit Profiles, and select your own profile.
Under Parental Controls choose Profile PIN.
Enter your password, set a 4-digit PIN, and save.
steps.result: Your profile can no longer be opened without the PIN.

steps.title: Stop new profiles being created
steps.why: Otherwise a child simply makes themselves a fresh unrestricted one.
steps.path: Account → Settings → Restrict profile creation
do: Open Account.
Under Settings, turn Restrict profile creation on.
Enter your password and continue.

steps.title: Turn on Kid-Proof Exit
steps.why: Makes leaving Junior Mode deliberate rather than accidental.
steps.path: Edit Profiles → Kid-Proof Exit
do: Go to Edit Profiles and switch Kid-Proof Exit on.
Enter your password.
steps.note: This only slows the exit from Junior Mode. It does not lock where they land, which is what the profile PIN above is for.

steps.title: Add a device-level backstop
steps.why: These settings only cover this one service. A device-level control catches the app they download next.
do: Set up Screen Time, Family Link, Microsoft Family Safety or your console's own controls.
Require your approval for new app downloads.
steps.note: SafeStart has a separate guide for each of these. Pick your device on the home screen.

checklist: Junior Mode on, or a content rating set
Kid-Proof Exit on for younger children
talkAboutIt: Junior Mode is all-ages, so an older child will find it babyish. Better to talk about why than let them work around it.
Agree what they do if something they start makes them uncomfortable.

kidsAlt.name: Junior Mode
kidsAlt.what: A simpler profile that only shows content suitable for all ages. The ceiling is fixed, so there is no rating to adjust and nothing to get wrong.
kidsAlt.watchOut: Kid-Proof Exit is a challenge, not a lock, so add a profile PIN to the adult profiles as well. Parents of 10 to 12 year olds often find Junior Mode too limited and switch it off, which leaves nothing in its place.

primevideo.name: Prime Video
primevideo.blurb: The controls are good, but two things trip parents up: viewing restrictions apply only to the device you set them on, and downloads from your profile stay visible in a kids profile.
risks: Viewing restrictions apply per device, so setting them on the laptop does nothing to the TV or tablet
Downloads made on an adult profile are still reachable from a kids profile
Setting the PIN does not by itself switch the restrictions on
beforeYouStart: Have your Amazon account password ready.
Make a list of every device the household watches on. You will need to repeat one step on each.

steps.title: Create the Account PIN
steps.why: This one PIN sits above everything. It locks purchases, overrides any profile PIN, and controls who can add or remove profiles.
steps.path: Your Profiles → Edit profile → Account PIN and locks
do: Go to Your Profiles, then Edit profile, and pick the account holder's profile.
Choose Manage next to Account PIN and locks.
Enter your Amazon details.
Choose Create next to Prime Video Account PIN, set it, and continue.
steps.note: Creating the PIN is not the same as switching restrictions on. On Android in particular they are two separate actions, so do the next steps as well.

steps.title: Make them a kids profile
steps.why: A kids profile only shows titles rated 12 and under, filters search, and blocks purchases outright.
steps.path: Profile icon → Add new
do: Hover over your profile icon and choose Add new, or use Edit profiles on mobile.
Name it and set it up as a kids profile.
You can have up to six profiles in total.
steps.note: Be aware of one real hole: downloads made on an adult profile, including an 18-rated film, stay accessible from the kids profile.

steps.title: Set viewing restrictions, then repeat on every device
steps.why: This is the trap. Prime Video's own help pages say it plainly: viewing restrictions only apply to the device that set them up. The settings screen does not look like that.
steps.path: Account & Settings → Permissions
do: On a computer, go to Account & Settings, then Permissions.
Choose the age restriction and tick the devices you want it to apply to.
Save.
Now do the same on the TV, the tablet and any phone they watch on.

recommended.16-17: Young Adults (16+), or agree it together

steps.result: Only content at or below that level plays on the devices you ticked.
steps.note: The five levels are Kids (All), Older Kids (7+), Teens (13+), Young Adults (16+) and Adults (18+). They map to local ratings, so in the UK and Ireland they line up with U, PG, 12, 15 and 18.

steps.title: Lock purchases
steps.why: Rentals and purchases are one tap from the same screen they watch on.
steps.path: Account & Settings → Permissions → purchase restrictions
do: From the same Permissions screen, turn on purchase restrictions.
On Android this lives under Settings, then Parental Controls, then Purchase Restrictions.
steps.result: Buying or renting now needs your Account PIN.
steps.note: Purchase restrictions do apply to every profile and every device, unlike viewing restrictions.

steps.title: Lock your own profile and stop new ones
steps.why: Otherwise your child watches from your profile instead of theirs.
steps.path: Your Profiles → Edit profile → Profile / Account PIN and locks
do: Go to Your Profiles, Edit profile, then your own profile.
Choose Manage next to Profile / Account PIN and locks, enter your password and PIN.
Switch Profile lock on and save.
On the same screen, switch Creation and removal lock on.

steps.title: If you watch on a Fire TV, set that separately
steps.why: Fire TV has its own parental controls, and nothing in Prime Video's settings covers them.
do: On the Fire TV device itself, open Settings, then Preferences, then Parental Controls.
Turn them on and set a PIN.
steps.note: Amazon states this outright: Fire TV parental controls have to be managed on the device.

steps.title: Add a device-level backstop
steps.why: These settings only cover this one service. A device-level control catches the app they download next.
do: Set up Screen Time, Family Link, Microsoft Family Safety or your console's own controls.
Require your approval for new app downloads.
steps.note: SafeStart has a separate guide for each of these. Pick your device on the home screen.

checklist: Viewing restrictions set on every device
Fire TV set separately if you have one
talkAboutIt: Explain that downloads on your profile are visible to them, so it is worth agreeing what gets downloaded.
Watch something new together rather than vetting it alone.

kidsAlt.name: A Kids profile
kidsAlt.form: a profile setting in Prime Video
kidsAlt.what: Shows only content rated 12 and under, filters search results and suggestions, and blocks purchases.
kidsAlt.watchOut: Downloads leak through. Anything downloaded on an adult profile can still be reached from the Kids profile, so PIN-lock the adult profiles too.

accounts.name: Accounts and email
accounts.blurb: Before the device comes the account, and this is where most of the surprises live. Including whether your child needs an email address at all, which on Apple they do not.
risks: A child on your account gets your messages and your call history. Apple says so on its own support page
An account created with an adult birthday cannot be supervised, and correcting it later is simple on some platforms and impossible on others
The account quietly decides what they can reach. On Android it decides which YouTube they get
beforeYouStart: Know their real date of birth. Every control on every platform hangs off it.
Have your own account password to hand, because you will be asked for it more than once.

steps.title: Give them their own account, not yours
steps.why: Sharing yours is the fastest setup and the one that causes the most trouble later. Apple's own words: you might receive text messages and voicemails intended for your family member, and your call history will include their calls. It runs the other way too, which is the part parents do not expect. And if family sharing ever stops, whoever owns the account keeps everything bought on it.
do: Check whose account is actually signed in on the device.
If it is yours, plan on giving them their own before you set anything else up.
On Apple, everything below assumes a Child Account inside your Family Sharing group.
steps.note: Apple publishes a page recommending you do not share an Apple Account, and it lists exactly what leaks: messages, voicemails, call history, music recommendations, book and podcast bookmarks, and health data.

steps.title: Decide whether they need an email address
steps.why: Parents keep asking us this, and the honest answer is that it depends on the platform. On Apple you can skip it entirely, which surprises almost everyone.
do: Apple: creating a Child Account lets you choose their own email address, a suggested @icloud.com address, or just a Game Center nickname. The nickname route means no email address at all.

Google: a supervised account normally needs a Gmail address. The one documented exception is a child under 9 on a Pixel Tablet, who gets an auto-generated @glimitedaccount.com that is not a working address.
Microsoft: you add a child to your family group by email or phone number, so an address they already have will do.

recommended.0-6: No email address. Use the Game Center nickname on Apple
recommended.7-11: No email address unless something specific needs one
recommended.11-12: An address, if school or an app requires it
recommended.13-15: Their own address, and you know what it is

steps.note: Google warns you may need to add a Gmail address later anyway for certain apps and services. Microsoft does not publish whether a brand new child account has to use an Outlook address, so treat that one as unconfirmed.

steps.title: Create it with their real date of birth
steps.why: The account type is set at creation and is not equally fixable afterwards. Apple and Microsoft let you correct a birthday, Google gives you a fourteen-day window, and PlayStation does not let you change it at all.
steps.path: Apple: Settings → Family → Add Member → Create Child Account
do: Apple: Settings, then Family, then Add Member, then Create Child Account.
Google: create the account through Family Link, or add supervision to an existing one with the child and their device next to you.
Microsoft: add them at family.microsoft.com, then give parental consent when prompted.
steps.note: The age at which an account counts as a child differs by country. Apple uses under 13 in the US, the UK and Canada, and under 16 in Ireland.

steps.title: Look at what the account switched on
steps.why: Creating the account turns things on that you never chose. Apple does not publish a list of what is on by default, so the only reliable move is to look rather than assume.
do: On Apple, open the child's iCloud settings and go through what is on: Mail, Messages, FaceTime, Find My, shared photos.
On Android, check which YouTube they have. A supervised account gets a supervised version of ordinary YouTube, which is not the same as the separate YouTube Kids app.
Turn off whatever they do not need yet. Adding something back later is easier than taking it away.
steps.note: Apple does publish the safety defaults: web content restriction and Communication Safety are on for under-18s, and in many countries Ask to Buy is on and cannot be switched off for an under-18.

steps.title: Write down what you set
steps.why: In six months you will not remember which address you used, which birthday you entered, or where the passcode went. The passcode is the one families actually lose, and on some platforms losing it means a factory reset.
do: Note the account address or nickname, the date of birth you entered, and where the passcode is kept.
Keep it somewhere your child will not come across.

checklist: Your child is on their own account, not yours
The date of birth on it is their real one
You know whether they have an email address, and why
You have looked at what the account switched on
The passcode is written down somewhere they cannot see
talkAboutIt: Tell them the account is theirs. Having their own is the reason your messages do not land on their screen.
Agree now what happens when they want something the account will not allow, so it becomes a request rather than a workaround.
If they are old enough to have an email address, agree what it is for before it exists.

imessage.name: iMessage and FaceTime
imessage.blurb: Already on every iPhone and iPad, with no minimum age of its own. For a lot of children it is the first place a stranger can reach them, and it is the app parents forget to look at because nobody chose to install it.
risks: There is no age gate. If they have the device, they have this
Communication Safety is a nudge, not an alert. It does not tell you when it finds something
Screening unknown senders sorts messages into another folder rather than stopping them
beforeYouStart: Turn on Contacts in iCloud first, because Communication Limits will not work without it.
Have your Screen Time passcode, not your device passcode.

steps.title: Set Communication Limits
steps.why: This is the real control here, and unlike most filters it blocks rather than warns. Apple's wording: if someone blocked by your limits tries to call or message, their communication will not go through, and it works in both directions.
steps.path: Settings → Screen Time → [your child] → Communication Limits
do: Turn on Contacts in iCloud first, or the setting has nothing to work from.
Set During Screen Time to the level below.
Set During Downtime, which can be narrowed further to specific contacts.

recommended.0-6: Contacts Only, and Specific Contacts during downtime
recommended.13-15: Contacts & Groups with at Least One Contact
recommended.16-17: Agree it together. Everyone is a reasonable landing point by this age

steps.note: The middle option is called Contacts & Groups with at Least One Contact. It allows one-to-one chats with people in their contacts, plus group chats where at least one member is a contact. Emergency numbers your carrier recognises always get through, whatever you set.

steps.title: Check Communication Safety is on, and know what it will not do
steps.why: It spots nudity in photos and videos on the device itself, both arriving and about to be sent. What it does not do is tell you. Parents assume this one alerts them, and it does not, so it is worth knowing before you rely on it.
steps.path: Settings → Screen Time → [your child] → Communication Safety
do: Confirm it is on. For under-18s it is on by default on current software.
For an under-13, viewing the blurred photo needs your Screen Time passcode, so that gate is real.
steps.note: It covers Messages, AirDrop, FaceTime, contact posters, shared albums and some third-party apps. The detection happens on the device: Apple never sees the photo and never learns that anything was found. For under-13s it prompts the child to start a conversation with you, which is the design. It points them at you rather than reporting to you.

steps.title: Turn on Screen Unknown Senders
steps.why: It moves messages from numbers they do not know into a separate list, so they stop arriving as notifications. It sorts rather than blocks, so treat it as tidying up rather than a wall.
steps.path: Messages → the icon at the top right of the conversation list → Manage Filtering
do: Open Messages and tap the icon at the top right of the conversation list.
Open Manage Filtering and turn on Screen Unknown Senders.
steps.note: This setting moved. It used to live in Settings, then Messages, and it was called Filter Unknown Senders. One documented hole: filtering stops applying to anyone they have replied to three times or more.

steps.title: Turn it off entirely if they are too young for it
steps.why: For a young child on a hand-me-down iPad, the honest answer is often that they do not need messaging at all. Turning the app off hides it rather than deleting it, so nothing is lost when you turn it back on.
steps.path: Content & Privacy Restrictions → Allowed Apps & Features
do: Open Allowed Apps & Features.
Turn off what they do not need yet.

recommended.7-11: FaceTime on for family, Messages limited to contacts

steps.note: Apple documents how this screen works but does not publish the full list of what appears on it, so check what is actually there on the device rather than expecting a particular name.

steps.title: Add a device-level backstop
steps.why: These settings cover Messages and FaceTime. A device-level control catches whatever they install next.
do: Set the device controls too, from the guide for their iPhone, iPad or Mac.

checklist: Contacts in iCloud on, and Communication Limits set
You know Communication Safety will not notify you
talkAboutIt: Tell them what Communication Safety does before they meet it, so a blurred photo is not a fright.
Agree that a message from someone they do not know is something to show you, not something they are in trouble for.
Show them how to block a number, and that blocking someone is not rude.

imessage.noKidsAlt: There is no younger version of Messages or FaceTime, and no minimum age either. They come with the device, so the only lever is the settings below, or turning them off until your child is ready.

hbomax.name: HBO Max
hbomax.blurb: Strong for younger children once you turn two things on. Out of the box the Kids profile is a suggestion rather than a lock, because a child can tap the profile switcher and land in an adult one.
risks: Kid-Proof Exit is off by default, so nothing stops a child leaving the Kids profile
Adult profiles have no PIN until you add one, and a new adult profile can watch everything
On phones, tablets and computers the app reopens on the last profile used, with no Who's Watching screen
beforeYouStart: Not available in Canada. It launched in the UK and Ireland in March 2026, and Sky and NOW customers there often already have the ad-supported tier included without realising.
If you are subscribing for Sesame Street, read the note on the first step before you pay.

steps.title: Make them a Kids profile
steps.why: A Kids profile filters the home screen and search as well as playback, so things they should not see never appear. It can never reach R or TV-MA whatever else you set.
do: Add a profile, mark it as a Kids profile, and enter their date of birth.
Pick the rating group for their age.

recommended.13-15: PG-13, TV-14 (ages 13+), which is as high as a Kids profile goes
recommended.16-17: An adult profile with a rating you agree together

steps.note: New accounts arrive with a default Kids profile already set to PG and TV-PG, which is aimed at ages 10 and up. If your child is younger, change it rather than assuming a Kids profile means young. Kids Mode cannot be switched off on a profile whose birthdate is under 18. On content: Sesame Street moved to Netflix in 2025 with worldwide premiere rights, so do not subscribe here for new episodes. Studio Ghibli is on HBO Max in the United States, where GKIDS holds exclusive US streaming rights. We could not confirm Ghibli for the UK and Ireland, so check before counting on it.

steps.title: Set the Parent Code and turn on Kid-Proof Exit
steps.why: This is the step that turns the Kids profile from a suggestion into a control, and it is off until you do it. It is the thing most parents are caught by, because the profile looks locked and is not.
steps.path: play.hbomax.com/parent-code
do: Set the four-digit Parent Code at play.hbomax.com/parent-code.
Turn on Kid-Proof Exit for the Kids profile.
steps.note: There is one Parent Code for the whole account, and it applies to every Kids profile on it.

steps.title: Put a PIN on every adult profile
steps.why: Kid-Proof Exit stops them leaving. A profile PIN stops them arriving. You need both, because by default a new adult profile can watch everything and the app reopens wherever it was last.
do: Add a four-digit Profile PIN to your own profile.
Do the same on every other adult profile, not just yours.

steps.title: Let the device do the rest
steps.why: HBO Max follows the device's own parental controls when those are stricter, which makes the device a genuine backstop here. It does not follow controls you set with a TV provider.
do: Set the device controls too, from the guide for that device.

checklist: Kids profile created with the right rating group for their age
Parent Code set and Kid-Proof Exit on
Every adult profile has a PIN
talkAboutIt: Show them their profile so it feels like theirs rather than a restriction.
Agree what happens when they want to watch something outside it, so it becomes a request.

applewatch.name: Apple Watch
applewatch.blurb: A watch for a child who has no phone of their own, which is the whole appeal. Apple renamed the feature to Apple Watch For Your Kids, so older guides call it Family Setup.
preinstalled: Messages and FaceTime, with the contacts you choose
The App Store, on the watch itself
Walkie-Talkie and Memoji, neither of which Apple documents a parental control for
risks: Fall Detection does not work for under-18s. Parents buy these partly for that and Apple only says so in a footnote
The watch is tied to the one iPhone that set it up, and has to be within Bluetooth range of it to change any setting
International roaming does not work on a child's watch, which matters for holidays and cross-border trips
beforeYouStart: Check your carrier supports it. Apple lists EE in the UK and four carriers in Canada, and does not list Ireland at all.
Turn on Contacts in iCloud before you begin, or you cannot set up the child's contact list.
Have the child's Apple Account password. You will be asked for it during setup.
If the watch is not new, erase it first.

steps.title: Check it will actually work first
steps.why: This is the step that saves a wasted evening. Apple's own pages disagree on which models qualify, and the carrier list is shorter than people expect. Ireland is not on it at all.
do: Confirm the watch is a cellular model. Apple's pages variously say Series 4 and later, Series 6 and later, or SE and later, so Series 6 or SE or newer is the safe reading.
Check your carrier is on Apple's supported list. In the UK that is EE. Ireland is not listed.
Confirm you are the organiser or a parent in your Family Sharing group, with two-factor authentication on.
A plan is not needed to set the watch up, but without one it only works near your phone or Wi-Fi, which defeats the point.
steps.note: Some corporate cellular plans do not support it either. Apple also says the feature is unavailable in Italy, Korea and elsewhere.

steps.title: Pair it to your iPhone
steps.why: The pairing decides which phone owns the watch, and that cannot be casually moved later. Use the phone that will actually be managing it day to day.
steps.path: Apple Watch app → All Watches → Add Watch → Set Up for a Family Member
do: Put the watch on and hold it near your iPhone, then tap Continue.
Hold your iPhone over the animation on the watch to pair.
Accept the terms, pick a text size, and set a watch passcode.
Choose the family member, and enter their Apple Account password when asked.

steps.title: Turn on Ask to Buy during setup
steps.why: The watch has its own App Store and a child can install from it directly. Setup offers you Ask to Buy at exactly the right moment, and it is easy to tap past.
do: Turn on Ask to Buy when the setup flow offers it.
For a firmer block later, use Screen Time, Content & Privacy Restrictions, iTunes & App Store Purchases.

recommended.0-6: Ask to Buy on, and installing apps set to Don't Allow
recommended.7-11: Ask to Buy on, and installing apps set to Don't Allow

steps.note: Same hole as everywhere else in Apple's world: Ask to Buy does not fire when they redownload something they already had. In many countries it is on by default for under-18s and cannot be switched off. Apple Pay with a card does not work on a child's watch at all, and Apple Cash Family is United States only.

steps.title: Choose who can reach them
steps.why: The watch's address book is a list you pick from your own contacts, not theirs, which is a genuinely good design. The limits themselves are the same Screen Time controls as on an iPhone.
steps.path: Screen Time → [your child] → Communication Limits
do: During setup, pick the trusted people to share to the watch from your own Contacts.
Then open Communication Limits in Screen Time and set the level below.
Set During Downtime separately if you want a shorter list overnight.

recommended.0-6: Contacts Only, and Specific Contacts during downtime

steps.note: Emergency numbers your carrier recognises always get through, whatever you set. Two gaps worth knowing: Apple does not document whether a child can add or edit contacts on the watch itself, and it documents no parental control at all over Walkie-Talkie or Memoji.

steps.title: Set up Schooltime
steps.why: It blocks apps and notifications during hours you choose, and unlike most controls of this kind it is honest with everyone: the child can leave it, you get told when they do, and there is a report of how long they were out. That makes it a conversation rather than a trap.
steps.path: Apple Watch app → Family Watches → [the watch] → Schooltime
do: Turn Schooltime on and tap Edit Schedule.
Set the days and times. Use Add Time for a split day, such as a lunch break.
Check the unlock report later rather than reacting to each notification.

recommended.16-17: Their call, with the schedule agreed

steps.note: Your child can see the same unlock report on the watch, which is the right way round. Schooltime turns itself back on when they lower their wrist.

steps.title: Set the safety features, and know which one is missing
steps.why: This is where the expectation gap sits. Fall Detection is 18 and over, so it does not work for your child. Apple states it only in a list at the bottom of the setup page, and a lot of parents buy the watch believing otherwise.
do: Turn on Location Services for Find My during setup, or the watch cannot be located.
Add emergency contacts and fill in Medical ID.
Check Emergency SOS under Family Watches, including whether holding the side button calls emergency services.
Do not count on Fall Detection. It is unavailable to under-18s.
steps.note: Crash Detection is on by default on Series 8 and later and has no stated age limit, so that one does work. Emergency contact alerts silently fail if Messages is not the chosen texting app or has been deleted. Also unavailable on a child's watch: sleep tracking, cycle tracking, blood oxygen, ECG, and international roaming.

steps.title: Set Screen Time for the watch
steps.why: Screen Time treats the watch as one of the child's devices, so the limits follow the child rather than the hardware. If they also have an iPad, one set of settings covers both.
steps.path: Apple Watch app → Family Watches → [the watch] → Screen Time
do: Open Screen Time, then Screen Time Settings, and set content, communication and downtime.
Set a Screen Time passcode that is different from the watch passcode and that your child does not know.

steps.title: Decide about health data and activity goals
steps.why: You only see their health data if they agree to share it, which is a request they can decline. Worth deciding together rather than assuming.
do: Request health data from the Apple Watch app if you want it, and let them accept.
For an under-13, set the Move goal to use move minutes rather than active calories.
Talk about rings and streaks before they become a thing they chase.
steps.note: Apple publishes nothing on what activity goals are appropriate for a child, and nothing on streaks and young children, so the goal you set is your judgement rather than a recommendation. Rings can be paused for up to 90 days without breaking a streak, which is useful if they are ill.

checklist: Carrier confirmed as supporting Apple Watch For Your Kids
Paired to the phone that will actually manage it
Trusted contacts chosen and Communication Limits set
Find My on, emergency contacts added
Screen Time passcode set, and different from the watch passcode
You know Fall Detection will not work for them
talkAboutIt: Tell them you can see where the watch is, rather than letting them find out.
Agree what Schooltime is for. They can leave it and you will be told, so it works better as an agreement than a lock.
Show them Emergency SOS and when to use it, including that it makes a loud noise even on silent.

outcomes.none: Nobody can message, call or speak to them on this app. Not strangers, and not their friends either.
outcomes.approved: Only people you have approved can reach them. Nobody else can message, call or speak to them.
outcomes.friends: Only people already on their friends list can reach them. Strangers cannot.
outcomes.teammates: Their friends, plus whoever the game puts them with. That includes strangers, for as long as the match lasts.
outcomes.open: Anyone on the platform can reach them.
